summary: Defines the multipart/form-data media type, which carries a set of values returned when a user fills out a form, and is used to upload files from web forms. It was replaced by RFC 7578.

eli5.summary: The way a web page packs your filled-in form, including file attachments, into one parcel to send.

questions: how are file uploads encoded in forms
what is a mime boundary in form data
how do browsers send form data with files
subtitle: A standard way to encode forms and file uploads for web applications.

tldr.problem: Web forms need to send text fields and file uploads to servers, but existing encoding methods did not label the type of each piece of data or support binary files.
tldr.mechanism: multipart/form-data uses MIME multipart encoding to wrap each form field or file in a labeled container, specifying its name, content type, and allowing binary data.
tldr.outcome: Web browsers and servers adopted this standard for form submissions, making file uploads reliable and widely supported.

facts.label: Primary use
facts.value: HTML form submission with file uploads

today: RFC 2388 was replaced by RFC 7578 in 2014, which clarified and refined the specification. The multipart/form-data format defined here remains the standard way for web browsers and servers to handle form submissions with files.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
HTML forms let users enter text, select options, and choose files to upload. When a form is submitted, the browser needs to send all this data to the server. An earlier method, application/x-url-encoded, could handle text but not files reliably and did not distinguish between different types of data.

RFC 2388 defines multipart/form-data, a MIME media type that lets each field or file be wrapped in its own labeled section. The browser assembles the form data as a series of parts, each with a boundary separator, a content-disposition header naming the field, and a content-type for the data.
sections.eli5: Instead of jamming everything into one long string, multipart/form-data puts each piece (like a text field or a file) in its own labeled box. Each box says what kind of data it holds.

sections.title: How the Encoding Works
sections.content:
A multipart/form-data message is a sequence of parts separated by a boundary string. Each part has headers (including Content-Disposition: form-data with the field name) and the field value or file contents.

For text fields, the content-type defaults to text/plain. For file uploads, the browser sets the content-type to the file's media type (e.g., image/png or application/pdf), or application/octet-stream if the type is unknown. Character encoding can be specified with a charset parameter for text fields.

If a form field can hold multiple files, they go into a multipart/mixed part nested inside the main multipart/form-data. The filename may be included as a convenience to the server for handling file references.
sections.eli5: The boundary string acts like a divider between the pieces. Each piece has a label (the field name) and a type (like 'text' or 'image'), and the file content itself.

sections.title: Integration with Web Standards
sections.content:
multipart/form-data follows the rules of MIME multipart types (RFC 2046). It is independent of the application using it: while HTML forms over HTTP are the most common use, the spec allows any application to use this encoding for sending form data via email, web services, or other protocols.

Browsers widely implement multipart/form-data for file uploads in HTML. The RFC notes that some applications may still use application/x-url-encoded for simple text-only forms. Servers should support both formats for compatibility.

The spec is careful about security: servers receiving form data must not overwrite files in their address space unintentionally, and applications must not cause users to transmit private information without consent.
sections.eli5: Browsers and web servers agreed to use this format for forms. It works not just for websites but for any program that needs to send filled-in form data, including file attachments.

sections.title: Field Names and File Attributes
sections.content:
Each field is identified by a name parameter in the Content-Disposition header. If field names contain non-ASCII characters, they must be encoded using RFC 2047.

Files can carry optional attributes: the original filename is included in a filename parameter so the receiver knows the original name, useful when files reference each other (such as a TeX document and its .sty style file). On systems with extended file attributes, the filename parameter can use RFC 2231 encoding to preserve non-ASCII filenames.

The ordering of fields in the multipart stream reflects the order specified by the form or application; the RFC does not mandate a particular order, allowing different systems to work in their own way.
sections.eli5: Each part says its field name so the server knows which form field it came from. For file uploads, the original filename is included so the server knows what the file is called.

fields.name: Headers
fields.desc: Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="photo.jpg" Content-Type: image/jpeg
